params.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with swelling of the right knee for 8 weeks. She has no fever or rash, and ANA is positive at 1:320. According to the ILAR classification, which JIA subtype is MOST likely?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic JIA presents with quotidian (daily spiking) fever and a characteristic salmon-pink evanescent rash — neither of which is present here.

Correct. A young girl with a single large joint involved (≤4 joints in the first 6 months), ANA positivity, and no systemic features fits oligoarticular JIA — the commonest subtype in India, accounting for 50–60% of JIA cases.
Polyarticular RF-positive JIA requires ≥5 joints in the first 6 months and is associated with rheumatoid factor positivity, not isolated single large-joint involvement.
Enthesitis-related arthritis typically affects older boys, involves entheseal sites (tendon/ligament insertions), and is HLA-B27 associated rather than ANA-positive.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the ILAR classification: a young girl with a single swollen large joint, no systemic features, and a positive ANA fits oligoarticular JIA — the commonest JIA subtype in India (50–60% of cases).

Oligoarticular JIA (≤4 joints in the first 6 months) is the most common JIA subtype in India, predominantly affecting young girls with large-joint involvement and ANA positivity — and carries the highest risk of silent anterior uveitis.

interactions.label: Which feature is the mandatory diagnostic criterion for Henoch-Schönlein purpura

params.question: Which feature is the mandatory diagnostic criterion for Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP)?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abdominal pain occurs in approximately 60% of HSP cases due to intestinal wall oedema and submucosal haemorrhage, but it is a supportive feature, not mandatory for diagnosis.
Haematuria suggests renal involvement (IgA nephropathy), which occurs in 30–50% of cases and determines long-term prognosis, but it is not required for diagnosis.
Joint involvement occurs in roughly 75% of HSP cases but is not required — some children present with purpura and nephritis alone.

Correct. Palpable purpura — raised, non-blanching lesions distributed symmetrically over the buttocks and lower limbs — is the only mandatory criterion. Unlike flat thrombocytopenic petechiae (caused by platelet deficiency), HSP purpura is palpable because IgA-mediated vasculitis causes perivascular inflammation and vascular leakage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key distinction: palpable purpura is the single mandatory criterion for HSP. It is raised above the skin because the underlying IgA vasculitis causes perivascular inflammation — unlike flat petechiae caused by platelet deficiency.

Palpable purpura is the hallmark and the only mandatory diagnostic criterion for HSP — it reflects IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis, and its raised (palpable) character distinguishes it from the flat petechiae of thrombocytopenia.

interactions.label: Why is the diagnosis of paediatric SLE typically delayed by six months or more?

params.question: Why is the diagnosis of paediatric SLE typically delayed by six months or more?

answers.text: Because complement levels remain normal in early disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Low C3 and C4 can be present even in early active SLE. The diagnostic delay stems from non-specific clinical features, not from normal laboratory markers.

answers.text: Because early features such as fatigue, arthralgia, and anaemia mimic common benign conditions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Individually, fatigue, joint pain, and anaemia are attributed to viral illness, growing pains, or nutritional deficiency. The diagnostic clue is the multisystem pattern — joint pain AND facial rash AND cytopenias AND haematuria together point unmistakably to SLE.

answers.text: Because ANA testing has poor sensitivity in children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ANA is actually highly sensitive (~97%) in paediatric SLE. The delay is due to non-specific early clinical features, not to limitations of laboratory testing.
While SLE is more common in adolescent girls, it can present well before puberty. The delay relates to symptom mimicry of benign conditions, not to age of onset.

overallFeedback.feedback: SLE's early features — fatigue, arthralgia, anaemia — are individually common and benign-seeming. The diagnostic delay occurs because each feature alone is attributed to a more common cause. The clue is the multisystem pattern: when several organ systems are affected simultaneously, think SLE.

SLE is the 'great mimicker' — its early features individually resemble benign childhood conditions. Recognising the multisystem pattern (joints + skin + blood + kidneys) is the key to timely diagnosis.

interactions.label: A 5-year-old girl with oligoarticular JIA has a positive ANA titre of 1:320. Her

params.question: A 5-year-old girl with oligoarticular JIA has a positive ANA titre of 1:320. Her eyes appear completely normal on torch examination. What is the MOST important next step?

answers.text: Reassure the parents that the eyes are normal and schedule routine follow-up in one year

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Torch and external examination cannot detect asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis. Delaying proper screening risks irreversible visual loss from band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, and secondary glaucoma.

Prophylactic topical steroids are not indicated without a confirmed diagnosis of uveitis — they carry risks of raised intraocular pressure and cataract formation. Slit-lamp examination is needed first.

answers.text: Refer for slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist every 3 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ANA positivity (≥1:160) in a child under 6 years with oligoarticular JIA is the strongest predictor of asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis. Slit-lamp screening every 3 months is mandatory — the eye can look entirely normal externally while active uveitis silently damages intraocular structures.

answers.text: Order anti-dsDNA antibodies to rule out SLE before any eye referral

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While anti-dsDNA helps evaluate for SLE, it must not delay ophthalmological screening. The immediate priority in this ANA-positive young child with JIA is detecting silent uveitis that can cause irreversible blindness.

overallFeedback.feedback: ANA ≥1:160 in a young child with oligoarticular JIA mandates ophthalmological slit-lamp screening every 3 months, regardless of a normal external eye examination. Silent anterior uveitis can cause irreversible blindness if undetected.

ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in a young child carries the highest risk of asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis. Slit-lamp screening every 3 months by an ophthalmologist is mandatory — even when the eyes appear completely normal on external examination.
